flashcards.q: Describe Aurora's storage replication and quorum model.
flashcards.a: Data is replicated 6 ways across 3 Availability Zones (2 copies per AZ). Writes commit on a 4-of-6 quorum; reads are served from a 3-of-6 quorum. Since 4+3 > 6, any read quorum is guaranteed to overlap a write quorum by at least one node, avoiding the need for full consensus on every read.

flashcards.q: Why is Aurora failover typically under 60 seconds while standard RDS Multi-AZ failover takes 1-2 minutes?
flashcards.a: Aurora replicas share the same underlying distributed storage as the writer, so failover is just a role promotion. Standard RDS Multi-AZ promotes a separate synchronously-replicated standby with its own storage volume and redirects DNS, which takes longer.

flashcards.q: How does Aurora Serverless v2 scale, and what changed in November 2024?
flashcards.a: It scales in 0.5 ACU increments, scaling up within seconds but scaling down gradually over several minutes to avoid thrashing. In November 2024 it gained scale-to-zero support: it can pause entirely when idle (only storage charges continue) and resumes in roughly 15 seconds on the next connection.

flashcards.q: Compare typical replica lag for standard RDS async replication vs Aurora replicas.
flashcards.a: Standard RDS replica lag is measured in seconds and can stretch into minutes (or worse) under heavy write load. Aurora replicas read from the same shared storage as the writer, typically producing sub-10ms lag.

flashcards.q: What is the DynamoDB per-partition throughput ceiling, and what's the observable symptom of exceeding it?
flashcards.a: 3,000 read capacity units or 1,000 write capacity units per second, per partition -- a hard ceiling regardless of table-wide provisioned capacity. Symptom: ProvisionedThroughputExceededException throttling on specific items/key ranges while CloudWatch shows healthy aggregate consumed capacity well below the table total.

flashcards.q: Does DynamoDB adaptive capacity eliminate hot-partition throttling?
flashcards.a: No. It absorbs some traffic imbalance automatically by boosting a hot partition's effective throughput, but it cannot exceed the hard per-partition ceiling (3,000 RCU/1,000 WCU). A genuinely too-hot key still throttles and needs a partition-key redesign.

flashcards.q: Give an honest assessment of DynamoDB single-table design.
flashcards.a: Works when access patterns are well-understood, stable, and the team has real DynamoDB expertise, minimizing round trips at high scale. Fails when access patterns evolve, since retrofitting a new query shape onto an already-overloaded PK/SK/GSI schema is harder than adding a table would have been. Most teams should not do it -- even Rick Houlihan, its original advocate, has publicly acknowledged the backlash against treating it as a default.

flashcards.q: Key constraint differences between DynamoDB LSI and GSI?
flashcards.a: LSI: must share the base table's partition key, can only be defined at table creation and never added/removed later, supports strongly consistent reads, up to 5 per table, shares a 10GB-per-partition-key-value size limit with the base table. GSI: independent partition key, addable/removable anytime with automatic backfill, eventually consistent reads only, up to 20 per table (soft limit).

flashcards.q: How much more do DynamoDB transactions cost versus a normal read/write, and when do you actually need them?
flashcards.a: 2x the capacity units of the equivalent non-transactional operation. Needed only for genuine cross-item/cross-table atomicity (up to 100 items, 4MB aggregate cap); for single-item idempotency, a conditional write achieves the same safety at half the cost.

flashcards.q: What happened to ElastiCache's default engine choice, and why?
flashcards.a: The Redis license changed to SSPL/RSALv2 in 2024 and added an AGPLv3 option in 2025, so ElastiCache now defaults new deployments to Valkey, a Linux Foundation-governed, BSD-licensed fork of Redis OSS 7.2. ElastiCache only carries legacy Redis OSS support up to version 7.2. Valkey is also roughly 8% faster, 20% less memory, and about 20% cheaper per hour.

flashcards.q: Name three real MongoDB features DocumentDB does not fully support.
flashcards.a: No retryable writes (app code needs its own retry error-handling), no $graphLookup aggregation stage, and missing or limited support for capped collections, GridFS, text indexes, vector search indexes, partial indexes, and client-side field-level/queryable encryption.

flashcards.q: When is a graph database like Neptune the right choice over a relational database?
flashcards.a: When the dominant query shape is deep, multi-hop traversal (fraud-ring detection, recommendation collaborative filtering, social-graph queries) where relational joins degrade as hop count grows but graph traversal cost per hop stays roughly constant. Wrong choice for workloads that are mostly single-entity lookups with shallow joins -- relational is simpler and cheaper there.

flashcards.q: How did DynamoDB's November 2024 price change shift the on-demand vs provisioned decision?
flashcards.a: On-demand pricing dropped substantially, making it the recommended default for unpredictable or lower-volume workloads (roughly under 10M requests/month). Provisioned capacity with auto-scaling remains meaningfully cheaper -- commonly 3-4x at realistic ~70% utilization -- for sustained, predictable, high-utilization workloads.

flashcards.q: How long do DynamoDB Streams records persist, and what's the operational risk?
flashcards.a: 24 hours. A consumer down for longer than 24 hours permanently loses those change records (unlike Kinesis's configurable longer retention), so consumer recovery SLAs need to stay well under that window, or a periodic reconciliation should back it up.

flashcards.q: Why does the primary in Aurora send redo log records instead of full data pages to storage?
flashcards.a: Redo log records are much smaller (tens to hundreds of bytes) than full pages, which is what makes a 4-of-6 write quorum practical across the network without saturating it -- shipping full pages to 6 storage nodes for every write would be far more bandwidth-intensive.
